newsitem.title: UK: "Rogue" trader risk has been reduced - ED & F Man.
newsitem.headline: "Rogue" trader risk has been reduced - ED & F Man.

text.p: The risk posed by "rogue" traders to firms and markets has been reduced in recent years by changes to the hedging environment and more regulatory awareness, said Charlie Hatton, a senior vice president of E D & F Man Group Plc.
His remarks on Wednesday were made at a company presentation during the London Metal Exchange (LME) annual "Metals Week".
They followed the scandal over losses by Sumitomo Corp of $2.6 billion, alleged to have been in unauthorised copper trades by a dealer active on the LME.

"The rogue trader danger is really less of a threat to any individual corporation or a systemic threat than earlier," Hatton said. "Are the risks more manifest today than when we first looked at them some years ago? I say categorically not."
But if another errant dealer were to emerge on the metal markets, the dealer was most likely to come from the speculative community, he added.
"There is a market sector worth taking a good hard look at, and that is the speculative community," Hatton said. "We could have a hedge fund disaster."
Hatton said changes to the hedging environment had gone some way to reducing risks.
These included a broader acceptance among companies of hedging, not least among world copper producers.
"Our research indicates that about 68 percent of copper producers had hedges on covering...1996 obligations," he said.
This covered them against the collapse in copper prices in May and June around the time of the first Sumitomo announcement.
There is also greater flexibility in hedging techniques, with more active than passive management.
Hatton spoke of a deeper understanding of hedging at every level of the company, right through to the shareholders.
He said important improvements had also been made to market regulation in the last few years.

Global co-operation between regulators, including sharing information on exposure, was one such development, as was setting public standards as a way of exerting moral pressure on participants to stick to the rules.
Individual markets have also responded to systemic risks, with membership shifting towards larger and more capitalised companies, particularly on the LME, Hatton said.
The introduction of LME average rate options in 1997 will further reduce risk by raising market transparency, he added.
"This has benefits for members as well as market users."
Further changes were under consideration for the metal markets which could further lessen the threat of errant traders.

They included the issue of credit lines and the possible introduction of cash clearing, better awareness of OTC (over-the-counter) derivatives and loan positions, and a breakdown of open interest on the LME.
Hatton said more information on LME stock ownership was another area where transparency might be improved.

He said the last few examples in the "rogue's gallery" showed a common theme among the people involved. All appeared to have big egos, wanted to cover up initial mistakes and became increasingly desperate in the process, he said.
Flaws in senior management oversight were also to blame, as were primitive risk management techniques, Hatton added.
"On the plus side is the outstanding performance of market mechanisms. There were no system meltdowns."
--Mike Collett-White, London Newsroom +44 171 542 8057
